lead: A VHF is simple to work once you know what each control does and what the set needs: a healthy supply, a sound antenna and a clear voice. Most "faults" on a charter yacht turn out to be a knob in the wrong place.

sections.title: What each knob and button does

qa.q: How do I set the squelch on a VHF radio?
qa.a: Turn the **squelch** down until the hiss starts, then up until it just stops. Set it any higher and it shuts out weak stations too, so you hear nothing for hours.

blocks.p: A fixed set has few controls. **Volume** sets how loud you hear others; it changes nothing in what you send. **Squelch** mutes the hiss between calls: turn it down until the hiss starts, then up until it just stops. Set any higher, it shuts out weak stations too, and you hear nothing for hours.

The **16** key takes you straight back to channel 16. The red **DISTRESS** button sits under a cover and sends a DSC alert: never press it to try it. **Dual watch** listens to 16 and one channel you choose; **tri-watch** listens to 16 and two others in turn.

blocks.rule: Squelch: just past the point where the hiss stops.

sections.title: 25 watts to reach, 1 watt close by

qa.q: Should I use 25 W or 1 W on my VHF?
qa.a: Use 25 W for range in open water and 1 W in harbour or to a boat nearby; the **H/L** key switches between them. If a distant station does not answer, check you are not still on 1 W.

blocks.p: The **H/L** key switches between high power, **25 W**, and low power, **1 W**. Low power is for short range: inside a harbour, to a boat nearby. If a station miles away does not answer, check first that the set is not still on 1 W.

The set lives on the yacht's battery. A blank display means no supply: check the VHF breaker on the switch panel, the fuse and the battery switch. A tired battery still lights the display but cannot give full power when you transmit, so others hear you weak. Run the engine to charge it, then call again.

lines: Engine off since yesterday, fridge running

qa.q: Does antenna height or transmit power matter more for VHF range?
qa.a: **Height matters more than power**: VHF travels roughly in a straight line, so a masthead antenna reaches much further than one on the pushpit rail, about 10–20 miles to another yacht.

blocks.p: VHF travels roughly in a straight line, so each antenna must "see" the other over the horizon. **Height matters more than power**: an antenna at the masthead reaches much further than one on the pushpit rail, and a coast station on a hill reaches furthest of all.

fig.note: The higher the antenna, the further its horizon

blocks.p: The cable is part of the antenna. A corroded connector at the mast foot loses most of the signal: range falls to a mile or two until you clean or replace it. And never transmit with the antenna unplugged: the power has nowhere to go and can damage the set.

sections.title: Short range, but it goes with you

qa.q: How far will a handheld VHF reach, and how do I get the most from it?
qa.a: Only a few miles: a **handheld** gives about 5 W from a short antenna at deck level. Stand up on deck, hold the antenna straight up and use high power.

blocks.p: A handheld gives about 5 W from a short antenna at deck level, so it reaches only a few miles. Give it its best chance: stand up on deck, hold the antenna straight up and use high power. Offshore, the fixed set is the one that reaches the coast.

rows: on the set, at deck level

blocks.p: Its strength is that it works away from the yacht: in the dinghy, and in the liferaft, so it belongs in the grab bag. Transmitting drains the battery fast: charge it before you leave. **IPX7** means it survives a short dunking, about 1 m for 30 minutes. It does not mean it floats.

qa.q: Why are my first words cut off when I talk on the VHF?
qa.a: The set needs a moment to start sending: **press, pause, then speak**. Hold the microphone a few centimetres from your mouth and speak in a normal voice.

blocks.p: You talk and listen in turn: press the button on the microphone to transmit, release it to listen. The set needs a moment to start sending, so **press, pause, then speak**, or your first words are clipped.

parts: press, pause, speak · release to listen

list: Hold the microphone a few centimetres from your mouth and speak in a normal voice: shouting with it against your lips distorts every word.
In a strong wind, shield the microphone with your hand or your body.
Release the button when you finish. A handheld jammed in a locker with its button pressed transmits non-stop and blocks the channel for everyone.
To test the set, ask a marina or another boat for a radio check on a working channel, never on 16 or 70.

blocks.rule: Press, pause, speak. Release to listen.
